newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Two of top Colombian magnates slam Samper.
newsitem.headline: Two of top Colombian magnates slam Samper.

text.p: The heads of Colombia's most powerful industrial group launched a tough attack Wednesday against President Ernesto Samper for his "lack of credibility" and "inability to govern".

"I would say (Samper's government) has extremely low credibility...Colombians do not believe the government is leading the country down the right path, including the path of peace," Nicanor Restrepo, chairman of insurance giant Suramericana de Seguros, flagship of the Sindicato Antioqueno conglomerate, told the Radionet radio network.
"There is a very real limitation and that arises from the lack of ability to govern," he added.

Restrepo made his comments after two other company chairmen from the Sindicato Antioqueno sent public letters in response to Samper's recent call to forge ahead with a new peace process to end Colombia's three-decade-old guerrilla uprising, which is estimated to cost the country the equivalent of 4 percent of gross domestic product each year.
The first letter, signed by some of the country's leading industrialists including Adolfo Arango, head of Cemento Argos, the main cement manufacturer in the Sindicato, backed Samper's initiative.

But a second letter by Fabio Rico Calle, head of the Sindicato's Compania Nacional de Chocolates, and published in local media Wednesday, questioned Samper's moral authority to head a peace process, saying: "We all want peace, but to achieve it one must have unshakable resolve, sincerity and moral authority."
In an interview with the Caracol radio network later, Rico was even more outspoken in his criticism of Samper.
"Samper may have good intentions, but at this stage it would have been better for him to step down from the presidency," he said.

Restrepo played down suggestions of serious differences within the conglomerate over whether the government should try and broker peace with Colombia's leftist guerrillas -- the most active in Latin America.

But he said that members of the Sindicato, which employs 80,000 people in some 200 separate companies with combined annual sales of $7 billion, were entitled to their individual opinions on the issue.
The heads of the Sindicato Antioqueno are traditional wary of media exposure and rarely give press interviews, let alone live comments on radio.
Elsewhere in the interview, Restrepo criticized the prospective candidates for the 1998 presidential elections for their failure to address core social and economic issues.
Rico was scathing of Samper's management of the economy, now plunged into its first recession in decades, but urged optimism to overcome the difficulties.
"The example we must set is of work and optimism so that the economy emerges from this dark night which began when Samper assumed the presidency," he said.
